title: Volatility
concept: Volatility describes how much and how quickly an investment’s price moves up and down over time.
learningObjective: Understand that short-term price movement can differ greatly between investments, even when their long-term results are similar.
primaryMisconception: Any drop in an investment’s price means the investment is bad or has permanently failed.
secondaryMisconceptions: A less volatile investment is always a better investment.
A highly volatile investment will always produce a higher long-term return.
keyTakeaway: Volatility describes price movement, not necessarily permanent failure.

screens.title: Same Finish, Different Journey
screens.content: Two investments finish near £1,200. One climbs steadily; the other crashes twice. Did they produce completely different results?
screens.illustration: Two paths begin at £1,000 and finish near £1,200. One resembles stairs, while the other resembles a roller coaster.

screens.title: Two £1,000 Investments
screens.content: You compare two fictional investments. Both begin at £1,000 and remain invested for five years.
screens.illustration: Two identical £1,000 starting cards appear beside separate covered price charts.

screens.title: The Staircase Path
screens.content: Investment A rises gradually. Its value changes by relatively small amounts and reaches £1,200 in Year 5.
screens.illustration: A gently rising staircase chart ends at £1,200.

screens.title: The Roller-Coaster Path
screens.content: Investment B rises above £1,000, falls to £850, recovers, drops again, and finally reaches £1,210.
screens.illustration: A sharp zigzag chart moves above and below £1,000 before ending at £1,210.

screens.title: Which Journey Felt More Uncertain?
screens.question: Which investment would probably feel more difficult to hold during the five years?

options.text: Investment A, because it ended at £1,200
options.response: The ending value does not show how stressful the journey was. Look at the size of the movements along the way.

options.text: Investment B, because its value moved sharply
options.response: Correct. Large rises and falls may create more uncertainty and make an investor more tempted to react.

options.text: Both were identical throughout
options.response: They began and ended near similar values, but their paths were very different.

options.text: Neither, because both finished above £1,000
options.response: The final result does not erase the large temporary declines experienced during the journey.

screens.title: Compare the Path, Not Just the Finish
screens.instruction: Compare both investments before, during, and after five years. Identify which one moved more and what its temporary declines mean.

educationalAssumptions: No fees, taxes, dividends, interest, inflation, or currency changes are included.
The displayed values are teaching examples, not market forecasts.
A temporary price decline may be followed by recovery, further decline, or little change.
A similar ending value does not mean two investments carried the same experience or risk.
Lower volatility does not guarantee a positive return.
Higher volatility does not guarantee a higher return.
The activity does not recommend buying, holding, or selling any real investment.

comparison: Both start with the same amount.
Neither future path is known at the beginning.
The final result cannot be guaranteed.

investmentA.observation: Investment A changes gradually. Its largest yearly movement in this simplified example is £50.

investmentB.observation: Investment B moves sharply in both directions. Its largest yearly movement in this example is £400.

afterState.comparison: The ending values differ by only £10, but Investment B experienced much larger temporary rises and falls.

options.text: Investment A
Investment B
Both moved by exactly the same amounts
This cannot be compared

learnerQuestions.explanation: Investment B moved by hundreds of pounds between some years, while Investment A changed more gradually.

learnerQuestions.question: When Investment B fell to £850, had it permanently failed?

options.text: Yes, every decline is permanent
Yes, because it fell below £1,000
No, the decline was temporary in this example
No, because every investment always recovers

learnerQuestions.explanation: The value later recovered and finished at £1,210. However, a real investment might recover, remain lower, or fall further.

learnerQuestions.question: Which investment may have been emotionally harder to hold?

options.text: Investment A, because it moved gradually
Investment B, because its large declines created greater uncertainty
Neither, because emotions never affect decisions
Investment A, because £1,200 is lower than £1,210

learnerQuestions.explanation: Large temporary losses may make an investor feel anxious or tempted to sell before the longer-term result becomes known.

config.importantHiddenDifference: The final values alone hide the journey. An investor looking only at Year 5 might conclude that the investments were nearly identical, although Investment B involved much larger movements and greater short-term uncertainty.

causeAndEffectChecks.possibleResult: Its price may recover, remain low, or fall further.
causeAndEffectChecks.question: What can be concluded immediately from the fall?

options.text: The investment is permanently worthless
It will definitely recover
Its future result remains uncertain
It must finish with a profit

causeAndEffectChecks.explanation: A temporary fall does not prove permanent failure, but it also does not guarantee recovery.

causeAndEffectChecks.event: An investor sells Investment B at £850 after buying at £1,000.
causeAndEffectChecks.possibleResult: The temporary £150 decline becomes a realised loss.
causeAndEffectChecks.question: What happens to the loss after the sale?

options.text: It remains only a movement on a chart
It becomes a realised £150 loss
It is automatically refunded
It guarantees the next investment will rise

causeAndEffectChecks.explanation: Selling at £850 after investing £1,000 locks in the £150 difference, excluding fees and taxes.

causeAndEffectChecks.question: What does lower volatility tell you?

options.text: It must produce the highest return
It can never lose value
Its price has moved more steadily during the measured period
It is suitable for every investor

causeAndEffectChecks.explanation: Lower volatility describes the pattern of price movement. It does not guarantee profit, quality, or suitability.

volatilityDoesNotDetermine: Whether an investment is good or bad
Whether its underlying value has permanently changed
Whether it will produce a higher return
Whether it is suitable for a particular person
Whether selling or holding is the correct decision

config.validationMethod: Check the three main comparison questions and all three cause-and-effect questions.
config.retryBehavior: Keep correct answers marked. Return only incorrect questions and show the relevant values from the comparison.

accessibilityAlternative.screenReaderInstruction: Listen to each investment’s yearly value. Compare the size of its changes, then answer the six questions.

feedback.success: Excellent comparison! You looked beyond the final values and recognised the much larger price movements in Investment B.
feedback.incorrect: Compare the size of the rises and falls during the journey, not only the starting and ending values.

screens.title: The Size of the Swings
screens.content: You saw two investments finish near the same value after very different journeys. Volatility describes how much and how quickly an investment’s price moves up and down. Investment B was more volatile because its changes were larger. A price drop does not automatically prove permanent failure, but recovery is never guaranteed. Volatility describes movement, not quality, suitability, or future return. It matters because large short-term declines can affect decisions and make an investment harder to hold.
screens.simpleSummary: Volatility measures price swings, not whether an investment is good or bad.
screens.illustration: The staircase and roller-coaster charts finish side by side, with the size of each movement highlighted.

screens.title: A House Price During a Slow Market
screens.content: A fictional home is valued at £200,000, then £180,000, and later £205,000. The temporary decline did not prove the property had permanently failed. However, an owner forced to sell at £180,000 would experience a different result from someone able to wait.
screens.illustration: Three property valuations appear along a timeline, with a sale marker placed at the temporary low.

questions.text: Two investments both gain 20% over five years. One experiences several 30% declines. What should an investor recognise?

options.text: Both had identical journeys
options.feedback: The final percentages may match while the paths differ greatly.

options.text: The more volatile investment guaranteed a higher return
options.feedback: Higher volatility does not guarantee a better long-term result.

options.text: The final returns were similar, but the short-term experiences were different
options.feedback: Correct. The more volatile investment exposed the investor to larger temporary declines.

options.text: The steadier investment was automatically better
options.feedback: Lower volatility may be easier to tolerate, but suitability and quality depend on more than price movement.

questions.correctExplanation: The more volatile investment exposed the investor to larger temporary declines even though the final gain was similar.
questions.misconceptionTested: A less volatile investment is always better, or high volatility always produces higher returns.

reviewChecklist.notes: The mission focuses on volatility as the size and frequency of price movements.
The mission distinguishes price movement, temporary decline, realised loss, permanent failure, and final return.
The mission uses adult investing decisions, five-year values, selling during declines, property values, and emotional decision-making.
The mission does not tell the learner to buy, sell, or hold any real investment.
The mission states that temporary declines may recover, remain low, or fall further.
All investments, values, and price paths are fictional teaching examples.
Selling, holding, anxiety, and reactions to losses are explained without judging the learner.
The mission clarifies that volatility does not independently determine quality, suitability, recovery, or long-term return.
The mission uses pounds, investment values, property prices, financial goals, and familiar adult decisions.
The learner compares identical starting values, similar final results, yearly movements, temporary declines, and realised losses.
The quiz addresses permanent failure, guaranteed recovery, higher-return assumptions, and misleading final-value comparisons.

reviewChecklist.item: Mission can be completed in under five minutes
reviewChecklist.notes: The mission uses three short story screens, two simple value tables, six interaction questions, and three quiz questions.

reviewChecklist.item: Language matches the target reading level
reviewChecklist.notes: The language is practical, clear, respectful, and suitable for beginner adults.
